title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). Outcomes were binary per task (validator pass/fail). Baseline (single‑pass) passed 299/300 tasks; guarded (GVR) passed 300/300 tasks. Contingency counts: n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Provider accounting shows stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and total model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial calls + 1 repair call). The preregistered hypothesis (target effect 0.10 with planned ≈80% power at N=300) was not supported due to a ceiling effect and minimal GVR engagement. We release the sealed preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support community extension and reproducibility.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to assist network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and remediation. Prior work reports that LLMs can draft device configurations but commonly produce syntax, topology, or semantic errors; hybrid pipelines that couple LLM generation with deterministic verifiers and localized repair (generate–validate–repair, GVR) have shown case‑level improvements. However, the NetOps research community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks combining realistic intent tasks, synthetic topologies, and deterministic validators that permit sealed confirmatory comparisons of defended pipelines versus single‑pass generation. We preregistered and executed such a paired, machine‑checkable study to test whether a guarded GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass LLM under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and focused studies document active work on LLMs for NetOps and repeatedly flag gaps in evaluation realism and safety. Representative findings include (i) feasibility of intent→configuration translation in limited settings, (ii) evidence that verifier‑assisted iterative prompting improves correctness in narrow datasets, and (iii) known LLM risks (hallucination, prompt injection, adversarial prompts) relevant to operational workflows. Prior experimental work often uses small testbeds or human‑in‑the‑loop adjudication and lacks sealed confirmatory designs tied to deterministic validators. These observations motivated our preregistered comparison that fixes generation variance via a shared‑initial design and isolates repair efficacy under an explicit repair budget.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary hypothesis. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256: a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass LLM on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). Design overview and shared‑initial semantics. The experiment used a paired binary design with a single shared initial generation per task: the first generation served as the baseline (single‑pass) candidate and was reused by the guarded condition. For guarded trials the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) was run on the shared candidate and, only if the validator failed, the pipeline was allowed up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This controlled design isolates repair efficacy: any guarded advantage must arise from an invoked repair because baseline and guarded initially share identical textual candidates. Provider accounting confirms this: stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}. Task bank and validator semantics. The deterministic task generator produced 300 synthetic, fully specified intent→configuration tasks evenly distributed across four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, required_sequence constraint semantics, and difficulty metadata. The deterministic validator implements the scoring rule "full_intent_constraint_validation" and returns score=1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION) only when all required constraints are satisfied; validator decision traces (validation_before/validation_after, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes) are archived per task.
sections.results: Execution accounting and per‑condition aggregates. The preregistered run completed per the design: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301. Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation) records stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}; thus the guarded repair stage executed exactly once under the preregistered repair budget. Primary confirmatory outcomes (paired binary). Aggregated counts are baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667) and guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table (guarded vs baseline) is n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 under the implemented exact enumeration; paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.01]. Diagnostic accounting of discordant episode and repair trace. The run produced a single discordant pair (n10 = 1) and exactly one repair invocation; both the per‑task raw outcomes and the repair provider trace are stored verbatim in the execution bundle. The authoritative raw results file is execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) and the execution manifest index (execution/execution_manifest.json) records per‑artifact paths and hashes; reproducible extractors can locate the exact discordant pair id and the repair provider trace SHA‑256 from those archived indexes. Representative example artifacts. For inspection we include six representative scoring JSONs and their shared initial response texts in the bundle (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json … task-000006-*.json). Those examples illustrate validator traces (normalized_configuration, required_command_count, parser diagnostics) and show that many tasks required no repair. Statistical power and sensitivity. The preregistered power calculation targeted detecting a 0.10 absolute paired difference at ≈80% power with N=300 under conservative discordance assumptions. The observed baseline rate (0.9967) violates that detectability assumption: with baseline near 1.0 the maximum achievable paired improvement is small and the confirmatory design is effectively underpowered for the preregistered target effect. The null result therefore reflects a ceiling effect rather than evidence that repair strategies could never help under other conditions.
sections.discussion: Null outcome diagnosis. Two empirical facts from the archived execution explain why the preregistered effect was not detected: (1) the baseline single‑pass generator satisfied the deterministic validator on 299/300 tasks (near ceiling), and (2) the guarded repair stage executed exactly once (repair stage_counts = 1), so the guarded branch rarely differed from baseline. Because most guarded trials reused the identical shared candidate, the paired test overwhelmingly compared identical outputs rather than repaired alternatives. Implications for benchmark design. To better reveal practical repair value, future benchmarks should (a) increase task difficulty distributions (raise required_command_count, dependency_rule_count, or include "very_hard" patterns more densely), (b) permit multiple independent generations per task to widen generator variance, (c) permit iterative repair budgets or richer repair strategies (more than one repair call), and (d) adopt stateful validators that model in‑flight dynamics and sequential side effects rather than snapshot semantics. Each recommendation follows directly from the provider accounting and per‑task validator diagnostics archived in the bundle. Reproducibility and deterministic sampling. The declared model configuration is execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) with declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null; in our hosted adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) a deterministic invocation mode was used so that shared initial outputs are reproducible under the same provider release and invocation semantics. Exact bit‑for‑bit reproduction therefore requires (a) the same provider release and deterministic invocation semantics and (b) use of the archived per‑call provider traces (execution/provider_calls/) and execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 0d841d29…). Limitations and external validity. Tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and the deterministic validator enforces snapshot intent constraints without modeling vendor execution idiosyncrasies or runtime side effects; we evaluated a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one repair budget. Consequently the experiment does not establish production generality across models, vendors, or stateful execution contexts. Operational interpretation. The study demonstrates that a sealed, machine‑checkable benchmark with deterministic validators can produce tightly reproducible accounts of generator/validator interactions and provider accounting. However, detecting practical repair value requires either more challenging tasks or a pipeline configuration that more frequently triggers repair; otherwise GVR activity will be rare and paired comparisons will be dominated by identical shared candidates.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and conducted a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported. Provider accounting shows the guarded repair stage executed only once (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline and conclusions about repair effectiveness are constrained. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable community extensions with harder tasks, stateful validators, larger repair budgets, and multi‑model comparisons aimed at revealing when GVR pipelines provide measurable operational value.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight dynamics, vendor execution idiosyncrasies, or runtime side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) limit sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain the confirmatory inference regarding practical superiority of GVR.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving planned exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider conditions recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the execution manifest.

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact artifact files that contain (a) the single repair provider trace and its SHA‑256 and (b) the identifier and full validator diagnostic excerpt for the single baseline failure episode are present in the archived execution bundle (execution/provider_calls/, execution/scoring/, execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and are authoritative; execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 0d841d29...) and the full artifact hash manifest index those per‑item records for retrieval.
